items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the number of people that, working with all available resources and technology, gives the highest standard of living”.
items.answer: Optimum population
items.markingKey: Optimum population: the number of people that, working with all available resources and technology, gives the highest standard of living. [1]

items.stem: Explain why overpopulation is not the same as high population density.
items.answer: Overpopulation depends on the balance between people and resources (including technology and trade); densely populated Singapore or the Netherlands have high living standards, whereas sparsely populated parts of the Sahel may be overpopulated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark definition; 1 mark example each [3]

items.stem: Explain the indicators that an area may be overpopulated.
items.answer: Food shortages and malnutrition; high unemployment and underemployment; overcrowded housing and informal settlements; pressure on water, fuelwood and soils; out-migration.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per indicator [3]

items.stem: Table 12.1 shows index numbers (2000 = 100) for population and food production in Country G: 2000: population 100, food 100; 2005: population 114, food 111; 2010: population 131, food 130; 2015: population 149, food 152; 2020: population 170, food 163. State whether the data support Malthus or Boserup. Explain your answer.
items.answer: Malthus: population is outstripping food supply, so food per person is falling.
items.markingKey: 1 mark view; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Table 12.1 shows index numbers (2000 = 100) for population and food production in Country H: 2000: population 100, food 100; 2005: population 112, food 105; 2010: population 126, food 110; 2015: population 142, food 114; 2020: population 159, food 126. (a) Describe the trend in food production per person. (b) Suggest two reasons why national data may not show whether people have enough to eat.
items.answer: (a) Falling: population grew faster than food production. (b) Unequal distribution between regions and social groups; food exports or imports; waste; prices and incomes; quality of diet.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark trend; 1 mark data [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Kwame argues that overpopulation is caused more by unequal distribution of resources than by population growth. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to technology and population growth.
items.answer: For: Global food production is enough for all; hunger results from poverty, conflict, waste and unequal access; HICs consume far more per person. Against: Rapid growth in the Sahel and parts of South Asia does increase pressure on land, water and fuelwood; resource limits are real in fragile environments. Conclusion: Both matter, but inequality of access and consumption explains more of the imbalance than population numbers alone.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “when there are too many people for the resources and technology available to maintain a reasonable standard of living”.
items.answer: Overpopulation
items.markingKey: Overpopulation: when there are too many people for the resources and technology available to maintain a reasonable standard of living. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “The optimum population of a country never changes.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It changes with technology, resource discovery, trade and expectations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain how technology can change the optimum population.
items.answer: New farming methods, irrigation, energy and trade allow more people to be supported at the same standard, raising the optimum.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the view (1798) that population grows geometrically while food supply grows arithmetically, so population will outstrip food”.
items.answer: Malthusian theory
items.markingKey: Malthusian theory: the view (1798) that population grows geometrically while food supply grows arithmetically, so population will outstrip food. [1]

items.stem: Explain Boserup’s theory of population and resources.
items.answer: Population growth creates pressure on food supply; people respond by intensifying farming (shorter fallow, irrigation, terracing, new tools and technology), so food output rises; necessity is the mother of invention.
items.markingKey: 1 mark pressure; 1 mark innovation; 1 mark example [3]

items.stem: Explain why Malthus’s predictions have not come true at a global scale.
items.answer: Technological change in farming (mechanisation, fertilisers, Green Revolution); trade; birth rates fell with development; colonisation of new lands; food production grew faster than population.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: A model based on Malthus assumes population (millions) doubles every 25 years from 1 million, while food supply (enough for millions of people) rises by 1.5 million every 25 years from 2 million. Values: year 0: population 1, food 2; year 25: population 2, food 3.5; year 50: population 4, food 5; year 75: population 8, food 6.5; year 100: population 16, food 8. Explain why Boserup would disagree with this model.
items.answer: Food supply would not increase at a fixed arithmetic rate: population pressure would stimulate innovation and intensification, raising food output.

items.stem: A model based on Malthus assumes population (millions) doubles every 30 years from 1 million, while food supply (enough for millions of people) rises by 1.5 million every 30 years from 2 million. items.answer: (a) year 90 (b) 53 million people

items.answer: (a) Food supply would not increase at a fixed arithmetic rate: population pressure would stimulate innovation and intensification, raising food output. (b) Malthus: famines in the Sahel or Ethiopia (1984). Boserup: Green Revolution in India; terracing in Machakos, Kenya (“more people, less erosion”).
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: “Boserup’s ideas are more relevant than those of Malthus in the 21st century.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: Green Revolution, GM crops, precision farming and trade have raised food output faster than population; global famine has not occurred. Against: Neo-Malthusian concerns: climate change, water stress, soil degradation, biodiversity loss; local famines (Somalia 2011) and food insecurity persist; innovation may not keep pace in fragile areas. Conclusion: Boserup better describes global trends so far, but Malthusian limits remain relevant locally and environmentally.

In Malthus’s theory, events such as famine, disease and war that raise the death rate and reduce population.

items.stem: Explain the factors that threaten food security.
items.answer: Climate change and extreme weather; conflict (Sudan, Yemen); poverty and food prices; soil degradation; water shortages; waste; pests and disease; dependence on imports.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a government policy that aims to reduce the birth rate”.
items.answer: Anti-natalist policy
items.markingKey: Anti-natalist policy: a government policy that aims to reduce the birth rate. [1]

items.stem: Explain why some governments introduce pro-natalist policies.
items.answer: Fertility well below replacement causes ageing and future population decline; shrinking workforce and tax base; pension costs; national security or cultural concerns (Russia, Hungary, Singapore).
items.markingKey: 1 mark per reason [3]

items.stem: Explain the consequences of China’s one-child policy.
items.answer: Fertility fell rapidly; around 400 million births were claimed to have been prevented (disputed); rapid ageing and the “4-2-1” family; male-biased sex ratio (about 118 boys per 100 girls at birth in the mid-2000s); labour shortages; human-rights abuses.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per consequence [4]

items.stem: Using one named example of a population policy, evaluate the success of the policy.
items.answer: Singapore’s population policies: TFR fell from 5.8 (1960) to 1.4 (1986); the pro-natalist phase has had limited effect, TFR about 1.0 in 2023; the government relies on immigration to maintain the workforce.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Change in TFR with figures; social, economic and demographic consequences. [5]

items.stem: Briefly describe the aims and methods of the policy, for China’s one-child policy (1979-2015) or another example of a population policy.
items.answer: China’s one-child policy (1979-2015): Most urban couples limited to one child; incentives (housing, education) and penalties (fines, loss of jobs); exceptions for rural families whose first child was a girl and for ethnic minorities; replaced by two-child (2016) and three-child (2021) policies.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Aims, measures, incentives and penalties, dates. [5]

items.stem: Referring to Singapore’s population policies or another example of a population policy, assess the extent to which the population policy has been successful.
items.answer: Model answer (Singapore’s population policies): “Stop at Two” (1972-1987) with penalties for larger families; then pro-natalist “Have three or more if you can afford it” (1987), Baby Bonus cash gifts, tax rebates, subsidised childcare and parental leave. TFR fell from 5.8 (1960) to 1.4 (1986); the pro-natalist phase has had limited effect, TFR about 1.0 in 2023; the government relies on immigration to maintain the workforce.

items.stem: A student writes: “China’s one-child policy was the only reason Chinese fertility fell.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Fertility had already fallen from about 5.8 to 2.7 in the 1970s under the “later, longer, fewer” campaign, and development also reduced it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why pro-natalist policies often have limited success.
items.answer: Costs of housing, childcare and education, career pressures and changing values outweigh small financial incentives; effects may be on timing rather than total births.

items.stem: Fig. 12.3 shows the total fertility rate in China: 1970: 5.8, 1979: 2.7, 1990: 2.5, 2000: 1.6, 2010: 1.6, 2020: 1.3, 2023: 1. A one-child policy began in 1979. Suggest why it is difficult to judge how far the policy caused the change in fertility.
items.answer: Fertility was influenced by development, urbanisation, female education and changing attitudes at the same time; it was often already falling before the policy.

items.stem: Fig. 12.3 shows the total fertility rate in Iran: 1985: 6.4, 1990: 4.8, 1995: 3.3, 2000: 2.2, 2010: 1.8, 2022: 1.7. A family-planning programme began in 1989. (a) Calculate the percentage change in TFR between 1995 and 2000. (b) Describe the trend in TFR before and after 1989. (c) Explain one demographic consequence of the change in TFR.
items.answer: (a) −33.3% (b) TFR was 6.4 when the policy began. After 1989: it fell from 4.8 to 1.7 by 2022. (c) Rapid ageing as smaller cohorts follow large ones; falling working-age population; possible imbalanced sex ratio (China).
items.markingKey: (a) (2.2 − 3.3) ÷ 3.3 × 100 [2] (b) 1 mark each period with data [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: Assess the view that anti-natalist policies are more successful than pro-natalist policies.
items.answer: For: China and Singapore reduced fertility rapidly; Bangladesh and Iran succeeded with voluntary family planning. Against: Anti-natalist success often coincided with development and had severe social costs; pro-natalist policies (France, Sweden) have kept fertility near 1.7-1.8, though Singapore and South Korea have struggled. Conclusion: Reducing fertility has proved easier than raising it, because policies that reverse rising costs and changing values are difficult, but success depends on wider social and economic change.

Values: year 0: population 1, food 3; year 30: population 2, food 4.5; year 60: population 4, food 6; year 90: population 8, food 7.5; year 120: population 16, food 9. (a) Identify the year in which population first exceeds food supply. (b) Calculate the shortfall in food supply in year 180. (c) State what Malthus believed would happen when population exceeded food supply.
items.answer: (a) year 90 (b) 52 million people (c) Positive checks (famine, disease, war) would raise the death rate and reduce population; preventive checks could delay it.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “anti-natalist policy”?
options: China’s policy (1979-2015) that limited most urban couples to one child.
The use of contraception and education to allow couples to choose the number and spacing of children.
A government policy that aims to reduce the birth rate.
A government policy that aims to increase the birth rate.
items.answer: A government policy that aims to reduce the birth rate.
items.markingKey: Anti-natalist policy: a government policy that aims to reduce the birth rate. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Singapore changed from an anti-natalist to a pro-natalist policy.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. “Stop at two” (1972) was replaced in 1987 when fertility fell well below replacement.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “China’s one-child policy was the only reason Chinese fertility fell.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain why some governments introduce pro-natalist policies.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Fertility had already fallen from about 5.8 to 2.7 in the 1970s under the “later, longer, fewer” campaign, and development also reduced it. (b) Fertility well below replacement causes ageing and future population decline; shrinking workforce and tax base; pension costs; national security or cultural concerns (Russia, Hungary, Singapore).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark per reason [3]

items.stem: Briefly evaluate the success of the policy, for China’s one-child policy (1979-2015) or another example of a population policy.
items.answer: China’s one-child policy (1979-2015): TFR fell from 2.7 (1979) to about 1.6 (2000s); rapid economic growth; but forced abortions and sterilisations, gender imbalance, ageing (65+ about 14% in 2021) and a shrinking workforce; relaxation has not raised fertility (TFR about 1.0 in 2023).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Change in TFR with figures; social, economic and demographic consequences. [5]

items.stem: Fig. 12.3 shows the total fertility rate in China: 1970: 5.8, 1979: 2.7, 1990: 2.5, 2000: 1.6, 2010: 1.6, 2020: 1.3, 2023: 1. A one-child policy began in 1979. (a) Calculate the percentage change in TFR between 1979 and 2000. (b) Describe the trend in TFR before and after 1979.
items.answer: (a) −40.7% (b) Before 1979: TFR fell from 5.8 (1970) to 2.7 (1979). After 1979: it fell from 2.7 to 1 by 2023.
items.markingKey: (a) (1.6 − 2.7) ÷ 2.7 × 100 [2] (b) 1 mark each period with data [2]

items.stem: With reference to a case study of a population policy, describe the aims and methods of the policy.
items.answer: Model answer (China’s one-child policy (1979-2015)): Most urban couples limited to one child; incentives (housing, education) and penalties (fines, loss of jobs); exceptions for rural families whose first child was a girl and for ethnic minorities; replaced by two-child (2016) and three-child (2021) policies.
items.markingKey: Marked out of 8 [8] using levels. Level 3 (6-8): detailed, accurate explanation with good use of examples or the resource. Level 2 (3-5): some explanation, partly developed, general examples. Level 1 (1-2): simple, descriptive points. Level 0: no creditable response. Indicative content: Aims, measures, incentives and penalties, dates.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the maximum population an area can support without environmental damage”.
items.answer: Carrying capacity
items.markingKey: Carrying capacity: the maximum population an area can support without environmental damage. [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A revision website states: “Overpopulation is only a problem in LICs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “A country can be both underpopulated and have areas that are overpopulated.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. HICs with high consumption may exceed sustainable resource use, as shown by large ecological footprints. (b) Correct. Brazil has sparsely populated Amazon regions and crowded cities.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “A country can be both underpopulated and have areas that are overpopulated.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain how technology can change the optimum population.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Brazil has sparsely populated Amazon regions and crowded cities. (b) New farming methods, irrigation, energy and trade allow more people to be supported at the same standard, raising the optimum.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: “Overpopulation is caused more by unequal distribution of resources than by population growth.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to technology, population growth and consumption.
items.answer: For: Global food production is enough for all; hunger results from poverty, conflict, waste and unequal access; HICs consume far more per person. Against: Rapid growth in the Sahel and parts of South Asia does increase pressure on land, water and fuelwood; resource limits are real in fragile environments. Conclusion: Both matter, but inequality of access and consumption explains more of the imbalance than population numbers alone.

Judgement: Both matter, but inequality of access and consumption explains more of the imbalance than population numbers alone.

items.answer: Preventive checks

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A student writes: “Famines are caused only by a lack of food.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A revision website states: “Neo-Malthusians argue that environmental limits may still be reached.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Amartya Sen showed famines often result from loss of access to food (entitlement), e.g. Bengal 1943, rather than absolute shortage. (b) Correct. They point to climate change, soil loss and water scarcity as modern checks.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Boserup’s ideas apply best to subsistence farming societies.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the factors that threaten food security.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Her work was based on intensification in pre-industrial agricultural systems. (b) Climate change and extreme weather; conflict (Sudan, Yemen); poverty and food prices; soil degradation; water shortages; waste; pests and disease; dependence on imports.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark per factor [4]

items.stem: A model based on Malthus assumes population (millions) doubles every 25 years from 1 million, while food supply (enough for millions of people) rises by 1 million every 25 years from 3 million. Values: year 0: population 1, food 3; year 25: population 2, food 4; year 50: population 4, food 5; year 75: population 8, food 6; year 100: population 16, food 7. A government policy that aims to increase the birth rate.

items.stem: A revision website states: “Pro-natalist policies always increase the birth rate significantly.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Many, such as South Korea’s large spending, have had little effect: its TFR fell to about 0.7.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the consequences of China’s one-child policy. (b) A student writes: “China’s one-child policy was the only reason Chinese fertility fell.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Fertility fell rapidly; around 400 million births were claimed to have been prevented (disputed); rapid ageing and the “4-2-1” family; male-biased sex ratio (about 118 boys per 100 girls at birth in the mid-2000s); labour shortages; human-rights abuses. (b) Not correct. Fertility had already fallen from about 5.8 to 2.7 in the 1970s under the “later, longer, fewer” campaign, and development also reduced it.

items.stem: Fig. 12.3 shows the total fertility rate in Singapore: 1960: 5.8, 1970: 3.1, 1980: 1.8, 1987: 1.6, 2000: 1.6, 2010: 1.2, 2023: 1. A switch to pro-natalist policy began in 1987. (a) Suggest why it is difficult to judge how far the policy caused the change in fertility. (b) Explain one demographic consequence of the change in TFR.
items.answer: (a) Fertility was influenced by development, urbanisation, female education and changing attitudes at the same time; it was often already falling before the policy. (b) Rapid ageing as smaller cohorts follow large ones; falling working-age population; possible imbalanced sex ratio (China).

items.answer: (a) −47.8% (b) TFR was 6.9 when the policy began. After 1975: it fell from 6.9 to 1.9 by 2022.
